W0.p: A general heading for good, admirable qualities of character.

W2.p: Good character traits are believed to enter a person's body at puberty.

W10.r: (Cf. Q40.) Missouri French: Carrière; Icelandic: *Boberg; Jewish: *Neuman.
W10.p: A general heading for kindness, showing gentle concern for living creatures.

W10.1.p: A saint is so gentle that he never swats away a fly or gnat from his face.

W10.2.p: A saint is so kind that he gives a calf to a hungry wolf.

W11.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Spanish: Keller, Espinosa Jr. No. 200; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
W11.p: A character is known for being generous and giving freely to others.

W11.1.p: A man who has given away nearly everything to beggars is finally asked for his spurs, and he hands them over, offering to be driven by the beggar's help on horseback to let the beggar ride.

W11.2.p: A king or ruler who is extremely lavish with gifts.

W11.2.1.p: An emperor feels a day has been wasted if he has not given any gifts.

W11.2.2.p: A king refuses to eat breakfast until he has handed out gifts.

W11.3.p: A man divides his money into three shares: one for the poor, one for pilgrims, and one for himself and his family.

W11.4.r: Wesselski Archiv Orientální II 429; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
W11.4.p: A man sells himself into slavery so that he can use the money to be generous to others.

W11.4.1.p: A Brahmin (a Hindu priest) steals in order to feed guests whom he regards as gods.

W11.5.p: A character shows generosity toward an enemy.

W11.5.1.p: A ruler forgives his enemies instead of punishing them.

W11.5.1.1.p: A man forgives those who attacked him, but they attack again and are killed.

W11.5.2.p: A ruler pardons a messenger who has come to murder him.

W11.5.3.p: A wronged knight defeats his enemy in combat and then forgives him.

W11.5.4.p: A conqueror sends a defeated man's wife and children back to him.

W11.5.5.p: A conqueror spares a captured city instead of destroying it.

W11.5.6.p: A ruler scolds his son for bringing him the head of a fallen enemy, and the dead enemy is given an honorable burial.

W11.5.7.p: A man is saved from harm because his enemy speaks up or pleads on his behalf.

W11.5.7.1.p: A man pays the fine for his enemy, who has been falsely accused.

W11.5.8.p: A captor contributes money toward the ransom of his captive.

W11.5.9.p: A warrior gives his horse to his enemy.

W11.5.9.1.p: A woman who has been falsely accused pleads on behalf of her accusers, asking that they be spared.

W11.5.9.2.p: A man who has ordered his own death sentence for a daughter he wronged is saved when she pleads for his life.

W11.5.10.p: A champion, when asked, grants his enemies safe passage to carry goods or travel home unharmed.

W11.5.11.p: A chieftain who catches his enemies off guard and unarmed lets them go instead of killing them.

W11.5.11.1.p: A chieftain who catches a king unawares spares him, on condition that the chieftain be called 'lover' by the women of the king's tribe.

W11.5.12.p: A hero in battle refuses to kill charioteers, women, or physicians.

W11.6.p: A ruler generously settles a dispute between a man who lost money and the man who found it, giving each a fair share.

W11.7.p: A nobleman's generosity lets a poor lover entertain the lady he loves in style.

W11.7.1.p: A poor nobleman offers his own wife to a ruler, and the ruler, sparing her honor, helps the couple.

W11.8.p: A general sends for the king so that the king gets the credit for a victory the general actually won.

W11.9.r: (Father had offered reward to anyone persuading his son to have it extracted.) Italian Novella: Rotunda.
W11.9.p: A prince gives away everything he has, and when nothing is left, he lets a man pull a tooth out of his mouth as a gift.

W11.10.p: A ruler shields a thief by taking the stolen plate and hiding it so it will not be found on the culprit.

W11.11.p: A ruler rewards a man who has offered to restrain or check him when he behaves badly.

W11.12.r: Ruler asks treasurer to give man 200 crowns. Treasurer makes error and puts down 300. Ruler raises sum to 400. “I can’t allow your pen to be more liberal than I.” Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
W11.12.p: A ruler accepts a correction from a subject and responds generously.

W11.12.1.r: Chancellor: “If you saw such a sum it would seem large to you.” King answers that it looks small and doubles it. Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
W11.12.1.p: A king rewards a knight with a large sum of money for correcting him.

W11.13.p: A generous man finds himself unable to give anything more away, the first time he feels his gifts have gone too far.

W11.14.p: A youngest brother shares his wealth with older brothers who foolishly lost theirs.

W11.15.p: A generous person never refuses anyone anything they ask for.

W11.16.p: A generous king gives away his only eye.

W12.p: Welcoming and feeding guests is regarded as a virtue.

W12.1.p: A king would rather die than lose his reputation for being generous to guests. He chooses death over being seen as an inhospitable host.

W12.2.p: A man goes out looking for strangers in order to offer them hospitality.

W15.r: Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 86 No. 756D*; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
W15.p: A woman takes in and protects the man who murdered her son, out of charity and compassion.

W15.1.p: The murderer goes to his victim's son and asks to be killed. Instead, the son helps him escape.

W16.p: A bishop trades places with a prisoner so that the prisoner can go home to his mother.

W18.p: A envious man plans to kill another man known for his generosity, but he is won over by the generosity of the intended victim and gives up the plan.

W20.p: A general heading for miscellaneous admirable qualities of character that do not fit the more specific categories listed in this section.

W21.p: An emperor who is friendly to everyone and treats others as he would want an emperor to treat him if he were an ordinary man.

W23.p: A man refuses to listen to gossip or slander about other people.

W24.p: A man never says anything bad about anyone.

W25.p: A comedian stays perfectly calm in the face of disaster. When a flood carries off his house, he keeps fiddling the whole time without concern.

W25.1.p: An enslaved man bears a series of misfortunes without complaining.

W25.2.p: A minister responds to every event, good or bad, by saying, "It is for the best."

W26.p: A general heading for patience, meaning the ability to endure hardship or delay calmly.

W27.p: A general heading for gratitude, meaning being thankful for benefits or blessings received.

W27.1.p: A man weeps with thankfulness to God because God did not make him as ugly as a toad.

W28.p: A general heading for self-sacrifice, meaning giving up one's own life or well-being for someone else.

W28.1.p: A woman drinks poison so that her son can become king.

W28.2.p: A woman gives up her life to protect her son's honor.

W28.3.p: A man jumps from a ship into the jaws of a sea monster so that the remaining passengers can be saved.

W28.4.p: A saint threatens to take the place of a murderer in hell unless the murderer's soul is released. The saint is willing to suffer in the murderer's stead.

W31.p: Obedience: a character follows orders or commands faithfully.

W32.p: Bravery: a character shows courage and fearlessness, especially in danger or battle.

W32.1.p: King Richard gets his army to victory by making his horse leap overboard from a ship, so that the men follow him ashore.

W33.p: Heroism: a character performs deeds of great courage or self-sacrifice for a greater cause.

W33.1.p: A warrior who is badly wounded keeps on fighting anyway.

W33.2.p: A warrior turns down a promise of a long, happy life in exchange for postponing a battle.

W34.p: Loyalty: a character stays faithful to a lord, friend, or companion.

W34.1.p: A man who has been forced to flee with his leader's fiancée refuses her attempts to seduce him.

W34.2.p: Loyal friends refuse to fight against a comrade who has fallen into disgrace.

W34.3.p: A man considers it cowardly to leave a battle while his lord is still alive.

W34.4.p: A holy man rewarded by a prince with a life of luxury in the city chooses to go back to his monkey friends in the jungle.

W35.p: Justice: a character judges fairly and acts rightly toward all people.

W35.1.p: A man is chosen to judge a bull-fight because he is no fairer to his friend than to his enemy.

W35.2.p: An honest judge refuses a bribe, saying he answers to a higher court called Conscience.

W37.p: Conscientiousness: a character is careful and faithful in doing what is right and what they owe.

W37.0.1.p: A man never breaks his word.

W37.1.p: An oil well digger runs out of money and leaves the country, forgetting to tell his driller to stop. He returns fifty years later and finds the driller still drilling away.

W37.2.p: A man keeps his promise to return to be eaten by a tiger, and so is let go unharmed.

W37.3.p: A rabbi returns a jewel that was found with a donkey he bought, because he had not paid for the jewel.

W43.p: A general motif of calm, peaceful temperament as a trait of a character.

W45.p: A general motif of a character who values honor and personal dignity above other concerns.

W45.1.p: A defeated soldier lying on the ground asks his enemy to stab him in the chest rather than the back, so that his honor is preserved. The captor spares him, and the two become friends.

W100.p: A general heading for stories about faulty or bad character traits.

W110.p: A heading for negative character traits that belong to a person's own nature rather than to their dealings with others.

W111.r: Types 368*, 675, 822, 843*, 1370*, 1405, 1454*, 1561, 1950; *Chauvin IX 33f. Nos. 25, 26; *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 30; Missouri French: Carrière; S. A. Indian (Chiriguano): Métraux RMLP XXXIII 175; West Indies: Flowers 581.
W111.p: A general motif of a person who is lazy and avoids effort, often to absurd lengths.

W111.1.r: *Type 1950; *BP III 207; Wesselski Märchen 213 No. 21; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 261; Oesterley No. 91; Fb “doven” IV 102b.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys.
W111.1.p: Several characters compete to show who is the laziest, each telling of instances of his own idleness.

W111.1.1.r: Wesselski Märchen 213 No. 21; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 261; India: Thompson-Balys.
W111.1.1.p: A lazy man lets his legs burn in a fire rather than move them out of the flames.

W111.1.1.1.p: A man is burned to death because he is too lazy to put out a spark that sets him on fire.

W111.1.1.2.p: A lazy man's belongings burn up because he is too lazy to stop rats from playing with a lighted candle.

W111.1.1.3.p: A man is too lazy to open his eyes, so he does not see the fire burning around him.

W111.1.1.4.p: Three lazy beggars choose to burn to death rather than run away from a burning castle.

W111.1.1.5.p: A mother calls out to her daughter that she is standing on a live coal, and the daughter is too lazy to move and asks which foot the coal is under.

W111.1.2.r: Wesselski Märchen 213 No. 21; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 261.
W111.1.2.p: A man about to be hanged will not lift a knife to cut the rope around his neck because he is too lazy to move.

W111.1.3.r: Wesselski Märchen 213 No. 21; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
W111.1.3.p: A man lying in bed will not move even when water drips into his eyes.

W111.1.4.p: A man is so lazy that he will not wipe his running nose, and this costs him a prospective bride.

W111.1.5.p: A man floating in a river is too lazy to drink, and as a result his voice is damaged.

W111.1.6.p: A man is too lazy to pick up berries or dates that lie near him.

W111.2.p: A servant who avoids work as much as possible, a stock figure of laziness in stories.

W111.2.0.1.p: A lazy servant gets other people to do his duties for him.

W111.2.1.p: A lazy servant is told to wake his master at dawn, and instead of checking the time he peers into a dark closet to see whether it is light yet. The note adds that such servants sleep until noon.

W111.2.2.p: A lazy servant leaves the door open at night so that he will not have to get up and open it the next morning.

W111.2.3.p: A lazy servant says he wants food if it is daytime and sleep if it is night, so he never has to work. The note says the master has told him to go to work.

W111.2.4.r: Wesselski Mönchslatein 54 No. 47; *Crane Vitry 216 No. 204; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: *Thompson-Balys.
W111.2.4.p: A lazy boy, asked whether it is raining, calls the dog or cat inside and feels its paws to find out, rather than going to look outside.

W111.2.5.p: A lazy boy, asked whether there is a fire in the house, feels the cat to see whether she is warm instead of checking the hearth himself.

W111.2.6.p: A lazy boy eats breakfast, dinner and supper one right after another so he does not have to eat again later, then lies down to sleep.

W111.2.7.p: A lazy boy always claims it is still raining, so he can stay in bed or in the hay barn instead of working. The note describes a peasant and the boy sleeping in a hay barn during rain, with the boy insisting it is still raining whenever the peasant asks.

W111.2.8.p: A lazy boy claims he is unable to walk so that he does not have to go anywhere or do chores.

W111.2.9.p: A servant tells his master to cover his own face so the master will not need the lamp put out, which is the servant's way of avoiding the extra effort.

W111.3.p: A heading for tales about a lazy wife who avoids housework.

W111.3.1.p: A lazy wife, still in her dirty dress, expects her husband to bring her a new dress from market, but he is bringing her a goose.

W111.3.2.p: A lazy wife is made to hold a cat while it is beaten for not working, and the cat scratches her in the process.

W111.3.3.p: A lazy wife, instead of putting the bread back into the oven, throws it out of the window.

W111.3.4.p: A lazy wife, beaten by her husband, insists she has done no work at all, and that is the reason he is beating her.

W111.3.5.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1370B*; Russian: Andrejev No. 1370B*.
W111.3.5.p: A lazy wife who has not spun her flax is beaten by her husband, even after he supposedly died and came back to life, because she had no shirt ready for his burial.

W111.3.6.p: A saying: whoever will not work shall not eat. The note says an idle daughter-in-law learns to work through it.

W111.4.p: A heading for tales about a lazy husband.

W111.5.p: A heading for miscellaneous tales about lazy people not covered by the categories above.

W111.5.1.p: A lazy mother is given cotton shoes, and her son knows she will never wear them out because she will not walk enough to do so.

W111.5.2.p: A lazy girl does not know where the spring is, because she has never bothered to walk to fetch water.

W111.5.3.p: A lazy man who is asked for directions only points the way with his foot instead of bothering to speak or lift a hand.

W111.5.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 381), 126 (ST 348); Halm Aesop No. 413.
W111.5.4.p: A lazy dog gets up only when it is time to eat.

W111.5.5.p: A man stuck in mud refuses to take the hand held out to help him up, because grasping it would take too much effort.

W111.5.6.p: A lazy son-in-law is so idle that he is afraid of a dog, because chasing it off or getting away from it would take effort.

W111.5.7.p: A ruler is too lazy to put a stop to quarrels among his people, and the quarrels eventually lead to his death.

W111.5.8.p: A man with a stolen fig in his mouth lets someone cut open his cheek to remove it rather than open his mouth to spit it out.

W111.5.8.1.p: A man is so lazy that he would starve rather than open his mouth to catch food that falls from the trees into it.

W111.5.9.r: starts making something big, which at the end turns to nothing. For example, begins with forging a plough: this becomes an axe, the axe a knife, and knife a needle, the needle—nothing. (Cf. J2080.) Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 2446*.
W111.5.9.p: A lazy man learns a trade while lying in bed, and when he later works on his own he ruins the materials he has been given.

W111.5.10.p: A lazy man will not accept wood as a gift until he has checked that it is already split, so he does not have to do the work himself.

W111.5.10.1.r: The lazy one rises up from the bottom of the wagon or coffin where he has been lying: “Is the corn shelled?” Canada, U.S.: *Baughman.
W111.5.10.1.p: A lazy man is being taken to the poorhouse, out of town, or to the cemetery to be buried alive. People take pity on him and give him things to help him get started again, such as a bushel of corn.

W111.5.11.p: A lazy man misses the sheriff's funeral procession because he is sitting facing the wrong way when it passes.

W111.5.12.p: A man digs three potatoes in one day, and the joke is that one is dug, one is being dug, and one is about to be dug.

W111.5.13.p: A man weeds his garden from a cushioned rocking chair, using fire tongs to reach the weeds so he never has to get up.

W115.p: Being dirty, untidy, and careless about personal cleanliness.

W115.1.p: A fiancée who is dirty and untidy in her appearance and habits.

W115.2.p: A woman only becomes clean after being washed three times and using three pounds of soap.

W115.3.p: A rancher cleans himself up at a hotel in town and is no longer recognized by his wife and family when he gets home.

W116.p: Excessive pride in one's appearance or reputation, leading to foolish behavior.

W116.1.p: An old woman reaches town ahead of a vain fop, who stops repeatedly to adjust his clothes.

W116.2.p: Spending money on things done merely to look good or impress others.

W116.3.p: Common people who are raised to positions of power show off in a vain, flashy way.

W116.4.p: A peacock admires its own reflection in a mirror out of vanity.

W116.5.p: A wasp, eager for fame, stings the courtiers and is killed for it.

W116.6.p: A wealthy man pretends to enjoy fine music so he will seem cultured; he is told when to applaud.

W116.7.p: A person uses unusually fancy or obscure language to display how well educated he is.

W116.8.p: A jackal makes all the animals that come to drink at the water praise him as if he were a king.

W117.p: Excessive bragging about oneself or one's achievements.

W117.1.p: A neglected wife is given a small trinket by her husband and brags about it to others.

W121.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Icelandic: *Boberg.
W121.p: Lack of courage; being easily frightened and afraid to face danger.

W121.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 67 (ET 314), 101 (ST 143); Halm Aesop No. 114.
W121.1.p: A hunter asks to be shown only lion tracks, not the lion itself, because he is too frightened to face the animal.

W121.2.p: A coward boasts of bravery only when there is no danger present.

W121.2.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI 56 (ET 166), 112 (ST 233); Jacobs Aesop 202 No. 9; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
W121.2.1.p: An ass insults a lion that is dying, daring to kick it now that it is harmless.

W121.2.2.r: Wienert FFC LVI 56 (ET 160), 112 (ST 232); Halm Aesop No. 40.
W121.2.2.p: A fox insults a lion that is caged, boasting safely since the lion cannot reach him.

W121.2.3.p: A crow sits boldly on a sheep's back but is afraid to sit on a dog's back.

W121.2.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 55 (ET 153), 112 (ST 235); Halm Aesop No. 219.
W121.2.4.p: Dogs tear up a lion's skin, yet they are afraid of the living lion.

W121.2.5.p: A coward gloats over a robber who was killed by someone else, taking credit for the danger he did not face.

W121.2.6.p: A monkey safe up in a tree insults a gorilla, calling it a broken face, though it would never face the gorilla on the ground.

W121.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 385), 137 (ST 425); Halm Aesop No. 379.
W121.3.p: A cowardly soldier turns and runs back when he hears a raven croak.

W121.4.r: “In truth, gentlemen, you do well in weeping; for since you didn’t fight like men to defend your land, it is suitable that now you weep like women on leaving it.” Spanish: Childers.
W121.4.p: A queen mother shames her cowardly son and his companions for their fear.

W121.5.p: A cowardly spider rushes at a fly but hides as soon as a wasp appears.

W121.6.p: A coward hands over his purse to a thief, making up a weak excuse to explain why he is not fighting back.

W121.7.p: A bridegroom who is a coward runs away when he sees an elephant and so loses his bride.

W121.8.p: A person becomes sick because of fear.

W123.p: A person who cannot make up his mind or decide between choices.

W123.1.p: A man who resolves never to drink wine but keeps tasting it, and so gets drunk anyway.

W125.r: Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; N. A. Indian (California): Gayton and Newman 67.

W125.1.p: A greedy animal eats fruit that is poisoned, even though it has been warned not to.

W125.2.p: A greedy wife eats the whole meal while she is cooking it, so none is left for others.

W125.3.p: A newly married son-in-law is offered a choice of meals and eats all of them himself.

W125.4.p: A pupil eats the cakes that were given as alms meant for his master.

W125.5.p: A husband eats his wife's share of food as well as his own.

W126.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman.

W126.1.p: A monk obeys only as long as the work he is given is pleasant, and refuses unpleasant tasks as beneath him.

W127.p: Peevish, sulky, or fretful behavior, complaining in a childish way.

W128.p: Being unhappy and never content with what one has.

W128.1.p: A hog tires of his daily food and asks the judge for better food, but a fox cheats him out of it.

W128.2.p: A dissatisfied fox, living in the kingdom of the lions, complains that he always gets the worst pieces of food.

W128.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI *75 (ET 408), 125 (ST 344); Halm Aesop No 380.
W128.3.p: Rivers complain against the sea, saying that its salt makes their water unusable.

W128.4.p: A peacock is unhappy with his voice, wishing he sounded better.

W128.5.p: A monk who is unhappy with his lot is told by someone that he should accept whatever God gives him.

W128.6.p: A sparrow, not satisfied with the water in a pond, decides it wants to go to the sea.

W131.p: Wasteful spending of money and property; reckless extravagance.

W131.1.p: A spendthrift squanders his whole fortune before he sets out on his own adventures.

W133.p: Behaving in a way that contradicts one's own rules or words.

W133.1.p: A prince punishes others for cursing even though he curses himself.

W133.2.p: A woman praises a hero's marvelous shot that kills a deer, then becomes angry at him when she pleads for the deer's life.

W136.p: Pretending to be modest or unwilling when one actually wants something.

W136.1.p: A peasant girl hides in a barrel when a nobleman comes to take her as his mistress, and when he is about to leave she calls out "Look!" because she really wants to be found.

W137.r: Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish: *Neuman; Icelandic: Boberg.
W137.p: Excessive eagerness to learn or see what is secret or forbidden.

W141.p: Talking too much or telling secrets by chattering.

W150.p: Heading for unfavorable character traits that concern how a person deals with others in society.

W151.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Icelandic: *Boberg; West Indies: Flowers 582.
W151.p: Excessive desire for wealth or possessions.

W151.0.1.p: A cauldron that never stops being filled, representing greed that is never satisfied.

W151.1.r: *Crane Vitry 214 No. 200; Herbert III 16; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 10; Scala Celi 87b No. 512; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
W151.1.p: A prostitute weeps when her poor lover leaves, thinking only that she has left him his coat.

W151.2.p: Visiting friends take everything from the house of a dying man.

W151.2.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *60 (ET 227), 122 (ST 311); Halm Aesop No. 131.
W151.2.1.p: Visitors to a sick stag eat all his food so that he starves.

W151.2.2.p: A hospitable man is made poor by greedy guests who keep coming.

W151.3.p: Wolves eat an ox entirely and leave nothing for its rightful owner.

W151.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 49 (ET 80), 134 (ST 396); Halm Aesop No. 345.
W151.4.p: A snake and a weasel, who are enemies, stop fighting so they can catch a mouse together.

W151.5.p: A man sues his father-in-law for breach of contract because the old man has not died within the two years he predicted. The joke is that the son-in-law wants the inheritance quickly, out of greed.

W151.6.r: “I intend to go there myself as soon as I get well again.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 215*.
W151.6.p: A hog with a broken leg refuses to tell another animal where peas can be found, even though it needs help itself. The greedy animal keeps the food for itself.

W151.7.r: The devil: “Don’t spoil the skin.” Shakes money out of the corpse’s throat and takes the skin. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3621, Legends No. 638.
W151.7.p: A greedy old man swallows his money before he dies so no one else can have it. Afterward, his son in church wants to cut open the corpse to get the coins back.

W151.8.p: Thieves start fighting among themselves over the stolen goods, and then the owner arrives and catches them. Their greed for the loot makes them careless.

W151.9.p: A greedy animal or person reaches into a food jar and grabs too much, so its hand (or head) gets stuck inside and it cannot pull free.

W151.10.p: A greedy man tries to stuff food up his nostrils as well as into his mouth, trying to eat as much as possible at once.

W152.p: A general heading for tales about stinginess, where characters refuse to share food, money, or hospitality with others.

W152.1.p: A fox ruins its own food rather than share it with an ape.

W152.2.p: A man would rather be burned alive than share his food with a guest.

W152.3.p: A stingy dead woman lifts her head from her coffin to correct a laundress's bill, because the laundress is overcharging her daughter.

W152.4.p: A stingy man is forced to share his money after he lies and claims he has none.

W152.5.p: A stingy woman refuses to give a man soup until she accidentally spills it. Only then does she say he may have it.

W152.6.p: A stingy king refuses to hire soldiers and is defeated in battle as a result.

W152.7.p: A spider living in a stingy woman's house grows thin because there is so little food for it.

W152.8.p: A stingy horse gives a donkey only a little feed and promises much more later, but never delivers.

W152.9.r: “It is better that they speak ill of me on an empty stomach than on a full one.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
W152.9.p: A stingy man cancels the invitations to his own guests, so he does not have to feed them.

W152.10.p: A drummer plays the drum at his own wedding instead of paying for musicians, to save money.

W152.11.p: Stingy men love their possessions so much that they wear out their own feet rather than wear out their shoes.

W152.12.p: A general heading for tales about a stingy master and the servants who suffer under him.

W152.12.1.p: A farmer gets his help up early in the morning and gives them only a glass of water and a lantern for breakfast.

W152.12.2.p: A stingy master promises his hired help a hot lunch to get them to work harder, but the lunch turns out to be a mustard sandwich.

W152.12.3.p: A stingy master orders his maid to whistle whenever she carries in dessert, because he fears she will eat the raisins out of the cakes.

W152.12.4.p: A stingy master makes his servants whistle while picking strawberries so they cannot stop to eat any.

W152.13.p: A stingy man mistreats his animals by keeping them short of feed.

W152.13.1.p: A stranger sees that a stingy man's cows are hungry and feeds them, and the cows die from the shock of being fed.

W152.14.p: A man is so thrifty that he insists on using every useful thing, even things others would throw away.

W152.14.1.p: A man finds a loose bunghole, the hole in a barrel, and has a cooper build a whole barrel around it so it is not wasted.

W152.14.2.p: A man saves his sausage skins and sends them back to be refilled with meat.

W152.15.p: A stingy man never eats his butter, but only looks at it and enjoys the thought of having it.

W152.16.p: The wife of a stingy man prays that her husband will fall sick so she can get better food while he is ill.

W152.17.p: A wife secretly keeps half of the money she was supposed to give for a shrine or religious offering.

W153.p: A person who is extremely unwilling to spend or give money, a miser.

W153.1.p: When a miser's strong-box is opened, his heart is found inside it, showing how completely his love of money has taken over.

W153.2.p: A miserly husband secretly watches his wife to make sure she does not eat too much, but he is burned in the chimney and beaten where he hides in the bed.

W153.2.1.p: A miserly husband spies on his wife to keep her from cooking too much food.

W153.3.p: A miserly wife is exposed to guests by her husband, who shows them how stingy she is.

W153.4.p: A man is so stingy that he will not drink wine until it has aged and become strong, so he gets the most from each drop.

W153.5.p: A stingy friar stays in a ditch for three days rather than accept help from rescuers, so that he does not have to pay them back by lending a hand.

W153.6.p: A miser dreams that he spends some money and in his sleep strangles himself out of distress.

W153.7.p: A miser decides not to hang himself, because he does not want to pay for a rope.

W153.7.1.p: A stingy man is so exasperating over the price of a rope that the seller hands it over on condition he hangs himself with it, as he had planned to do anyway.

W153.8.p: A stingy man names himself as the only heir to his own property, so that no one else can inherit it.

W153.9.r: Refuses to pay fee. Chain of circumstances make it infinitely more expensive. Italian Novella: Rotunda.
W153.9.p: A stingy man decides to slaughter his pigs himself rather than pay someone else to do it.

W153.10.p: A friend scolds a miser that his wealth does him no good, and the miser's foolishness is thereby shown.

W153.11.p: A miser dies because he refuses to spend money on a candle, so he is left in the dark or cannot see to die properly.

W153.11.1.p: On his deathbed, a miser tells his son to put out the candle the moment he dies, so no light is wasted.

W153.11.2.p: A miser runs back home to put out a lamp he left burning, even though it costs him his life or his chance to escape.

W153.12.p: A stingy man is kidnapped and held until a ransom is paid for his return.

W153.13.p: A wood seller prays that the king will die soon, so he can sell sandalwood for the funeral pyre.

W153.14.p: A stingy man tries to cut down the sacrifice he promised to a god.

W153.15.p: A miser prays to enter heaven still wearing his clothes, which have gold coins sewn into the lining.

W154.p: A general heading for stories about ungrateful people who repay kindness with harm or meanness.

W154.1.p: A servant who has worked for years is dismissed and given only a meager payment.

W154.1.1.p: A moneylender dismisses his servant and then charges him for a rope, even though the servant had cut the rope to save the moneylender from hanging.

W154.2.p: A monster or creature is ungrateful to the person who rescued it.

W154.2.1.p: An animal that has been rescued threatens the person who rescued it.

W154.2.2.p: A man is ungrateful after being rescued by an animal.

W154.3.r: B382.) *Type 76; *Crane Vitry 192 No. 136; *Wienert FFC LVI 54 n. 3 (ET 145), 147 (ST 517); Halm Aesop No. 276; Jacobs Aesop 200 No. 5.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
W154.3.p: A crane pulls a bone out of a wolf's throat, and the wolf refuses to pay him, saying it is reward enough that the crane was allowed to remove its beak unharmed.

W154.3.1.r: Cf. Type 75. Italian Novella: Rotunda; Africa (Ibo, Nigeria): Thomas 86, (Kaffir): Kidd 243 No. 10 (lion and gazelle); West Indies: Flowers 582.
W154.3.1.p: A lion caught in a net is freed by a rat, and then the lion eats the rat.

W154.3.2.p: A tiger has a thorn pulled from its paw by a man, and then the tiger attacks the man.

W154.4.r: Wienert FFC LVI 73 (ET 380), 89 (ST 14); Spanish Exempla: Keller. Cf. Type 101.
W154.4.p: A hunter turns against his dog after it has grown old in his service and beats it instead of rewarding it.

W154.5.r: Wienert FFC LVI 72 (ET 370), 147 (ST 523); Halm Aesop No. 192.
W154.5.p: A dog that has been pulled out of a well by a man tries to bite the man who saved it.

W154.5.1.p: A fox that a man has carried across a stream strikes the man with its tail as thanks.

W154.5.1.1.p: A man rescues a whale that carried him home across the sea, and then kills it.

W154.5.1.2.p: A man who has been rescued from a pit tries to kill the monkey that rescued him, in order to eat it.

W154.5.1.3.p: A monkey that a heron has carried across water repays the heron by plucking out its feathers.

W154.6.r: Wienert FFC LVI *74 (ET 394), 147 (ST 520); Halm Aesop No. 188.
W154.6.p: A traveler who wants the nuts tears a nut tree apart, ignoring that the tree gave him its fruit.

W154.7.r: Wienert FFC LVI *74 (ET 396), 147 (ST 519); Halm Aesop No. 313.
W154.7.p: Travelers resting in the shade of a plane tree blame the tree for not bearing fruit, though it gave them shade.

W154.8.r: *Type 160; Chauvin II 106 No. 71; *Penzer V 157 n. 1; Cosquin Études 22ff.; Moe Samlede Skrifter I 192ff.; *BP IV 139; *Wesselski Theorie 82ff.; *Oesterley No. 119; Fb “ulvgrav”; Bødker Exempler 304 No. 25.—Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas@2 IV 51, 277, Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Africa: Frobenius Atlantis IX 385f. Nos. 103, 104, (Gold Coast): Barker and Sinclair 163 No. 32, (Zanzibar): Bateman 81ff. No. 6.
W154.8.p: A traveler rescues several animals and a jeweler from a pit; the animals repay him generously while the man he saved betrays him. A monkey gives him fruit, a tiger gives him a necklace taken from a princess the tiger killed, the jeweler accuses him before the king, and a serpent saves him by biting the prince and then showing him the remedy.

W154.9.p: A man who has been saved from drowning kills the person who rescued him.

W154.9.1.r: Polynesia: Beckwith Myth 502—05; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/912).
W154.9.1.p: A king who plans to kill whales is saved from drowning by them.

W154.10.p: A snake kills the man who tamed it, because he has been ungrateful to it.

W154.11.p: A tiger returns a rope to the man who once held it captive, and is rewarded by having its tail cut off.

W154.12.p: A man kills the person who rescued him so that he can collect the reward himself.

W154.12.1.p: A knight, after being rescued in battle, shows no gratitude to the man who saved him.

W154.12.2.p: A Brahmin who has been helped by a wild goose takes the goose to the king as a cure for leprosy, to claim the reward for himself.

W154.12.3.p: Brothers who owe their lives to a rescuer plot to kill him.

W154.13.p: A young man who has been helped by a benefactor falsely accuses him of theft.

W154.14.p: A woman saves a suitor's life, and he later condemns her to death.

W154.15.p: A kind magistrate gives a lawbreaker a light sentence, and the man repays him by seducing the magistrate's wife.

W154.16.p: A ruler punishes or mistreats the friends who have served him and shows kindness to his enemies.

W154.17.p: A man cuts off the head of the person who rescued him because the rescuer left him in pain for too long.

W154.18.p: A man who has been saved is ungrateful because his rescuer also helped other people.

W154.19.p: A Jew who has borrowed a Christian's horse steals it from him, showing ingratitude for the loan.

W154.20.p: A man beats the people who bring him gifts.

W154.21.r: (Cf. W181.2.) Krappe “Les funérailles d’Alaric” Annuaire de l’institut de philologie et d’histoire orientales et slaves VII (1939—44) 229ff.
W154.21.p: The workers who built a secret building or grave are killed once it is finished, so no one else will know where it is.

W154.22.p: A person is compared to a nettle, which stings the hand that tries to protect it.

W154.23.p: Someone shows ingratitude simply because they do not understand what was done for them.

W154.24.p: A man fails to feed the animal that rescued or helped him.

W154.25.p: A bear carries a man home to safety, and the man then sets dogs on the bear.

W154.26.p: A man keeps asking for bigger and bigger gifts in return for his help.

W154.26.1.p: A trader swaps an egg for a needle and then demands a gill of rum, the usual reward for traders. The storekeeper gives him the rum, and he asks for an egg in it; the storekeeper breaks in the egg he just traded for the needle, which has two yolks, so the trader asks for two needles.

W154.27.p: A man works his own horses to death and then complains that a borrowed horse eats too much.

W154.28.p: A wizard makes his pupil believe he has become emperor, then reveals the pupil's ingratitude.

W155.r: England, U.S.: Baughman; West Indies: Flowers 583.
W155.p: A general heading for cruelty and lack of pity, where a character is unmoved by the suffering of others.

W155.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *56 (ET 170), 144 (ST 397); Halm Aesop No. 177.
W155.1.p: A hardhearted horse lets a donkey be overloaded until it collapses under the weight, and then the horse has to carry the load itself.

W155.1.1.p: An old bullock is abandoned and left to die after years of work.

W155.1.2.p: A man overloads his camel and starves it.

W155.2.p: A man helping another across a stream drops him when he learns the other has lost his high position.

W155.3.p: A man is so hardhearted that he cannot weep, even when weeping would be expected.

W155.4.p: A cruel, unforgiving person refuses to pardon the men who murdered his father, even when offered a reprieve.

W155.5.p: A hardhearted person refuses to let someone drink from a water tank, even when asked.

W156.r: Wienert FFC LVI 54, 58 (ET 142, 195), 132, 147 (ST 385, 518); Halm Aesop No. 228; Phaedrus I No. 19; Hervieux II 11; Herbert III 14; Crane Vitry 201 No. 161; Jacobs Aesop 209 No. 40.
W156.p: A selfish person who has no use for something still refuses to let anyone else have it, like a dog lying in a manger that the horse cannot eat from.

W157.r: Irish: Beal XXI 327, O’Suilleabhain 75; Icelandic: *Boberg; India: Thompson-Balys.
W157.p: A general trait of being dishonest or deceitful in one's dealings with others.

W157.1.p: A priest uses money he got through dishonest means to build monuments honoring himself.

W158.p: A general trait of being unwelcoming to guests and refusing to offer hospitality to travelers.

W161.p: A general trait of loving attention, fame, and being seen or praised by others.

W161.1.p: Three messengers sent on a mission argue over which of them should be given the greatest welcome and honor.

W165.p: A son is ashamed of his poor peasant father, who brings him money, and so the father cuts him out of the inheritance.

W165.1.p: A humble man who has spoken with a king becomes so proud that he looks down on his own family.

W165.2.p: A donkey that has kept company with a lion becomes so proud that it looks down on other donkeys, its own kind.

W167.p: A general trait of being obstinate and refusing to yield or change one's mind.

W167.1.p: Two stubborn goats meet on a narrow bridge, and neither will step aside, so both fall into the water.

W167.2.p: A woman's stubbornness makes her lose the chance to go on a pilgrimage.

W171.p: A general trait of being two-faced, pretending to be friendly to opposing sides while being false to both.

W171.1.p: A man winks at both the buyer and the seller, trying to seem friendly to each of them.

W175.p: A general trait of being fickle, with loyalty and affection that shift according to circumstances.

W175.1.p: A sister honors and values her brother only while he is prosperous, and drops him when his fortunes fall.

W181.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. Nos. 142—45.
W181.p: A general trait of resenting others for their good fortune or advantages.

W181.1.r: Wienert FFC LVI *58 (ET 197), 132 (ST 386); Halm Aesop No. 317.
W181.1.p: Sheep envy a dog because the dog seems to do nothing, not realizing the dog guards the flock.

W181.2.r: (Cf. S161.0.1, W154.21.) Wesselski Theorie 15; Ireland, England: Baughman.
W181.2.p: A king has the architect who built a magnificent building killed, so that no one can ever build anything as great again. Out of jealousy, he removes the one man who could match him.

W181.2.1.p: An architect kills his own apprentice because the apprentice has become more skilled than he is. Jealousy of a rival's talent leads him to murder.

W181.2.2.p: An architect kills himself on learning that his pupil has surpassed him in skill. He cannot bear being outdone.

W181.3.r: Wienert FFC LVI *46 (ET 49), 90 (ST 26); Halm Aesop No. 206.
W181.3.p: A raven envies the swan and wishes to become as white as one. Jealousy makes him want what another creature has.

W181.4.p: A jealous fox informs on a wolf to a peasant, then takes over the wolf's den and food for himself. The peasant kills the wolf within a few days, and the fox's treachery leads to his own downfall.

W181.5.p: A raven is jealous of the way a partridge flies and envies its manner of flight.

W181.6.p: Venus is jealous of the love between Psyche and Cupid and works against them out of envy.

W181.7.p: A ruler who begrudges his subjects their happiness forbids them to hold their games and amusements.

W182.r: *Crane Vitry 265 No. 300; Herbert III 13 No. 85; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 594; Scala Celi 158b No. 892.
W182.p: A child cries, then stops for a rest so that, after resting, he can cry even louder than before.

W185.p: A person with a violent, quick temper who readily flies into rage.

W185.1.p: A man overhears someone describing his temper, then storms in angrily to demonstrate it by demanding when he has ever lost his temper.

W185.2.r: Crane Vitry 48 No. 103; Mensa Philosophica No. 143.
W185.2.p: A prayer that an overbearing knight's illness be made worse. The reasoning is that a little sickness has softened him, so more might make him kinder still.

W185.3.p: A man loses his temper from reading history and becomes so angry that he refuses to pay his workmen.

W185.4.p: A monk loses his temper over a cup and smashes it in anger.

W185.5.p: A judge's violent temper causes him to unjustly sentence men to death.

W185.6.r: The lion to the man: “The wound has healed, but the pain of harsh words still remains.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 161*; Rumanian: Schullerus FFC LXXVIII No. 159IV*; India: Thompson-Balys.
W185.6.p: An insult is more painful than a physical wound.

W187.p: Rude, disrespectful, or insolent behavior toward others.

W188.p: A habit of quarreling and arguing stubbornly with others.

W193.p: Demanding unjust or excessive payment from others by force or threat.

W193.1.p: A man charges a drug addict an exorbitant price for a betel leaf, taking advantage of the addict's craving.

W195.p: Envy: a character feels resentment or jealousy toward someone else's good fortune or qualities.

W195.1.p: A goose and a turkey, jealous of a peacock, point out that its legs are ugly and its voice is harsh.

W196.p: A character is impatient and cannot wait calmly for things to happen.

W200.p: Miscellaneous traits of character that do not fit the other categories.

W211.p: A character has a vivid imagination, often seeing or reasoning about things that are not really there or imagining elaborate outcomes.

W211.1.p: A boy reasons that if he has one thing and then gets two more, he will have three, as if counting his imagined gains as already certain.

W211.2.r: “There weren’t so many as that.”—“Well, what made the noise in the bushes?” Type 2009*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1863*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 2009*; Russian: Andrejev No. 2009; India: *Thompson-Balys.
W211.2.p: A character claims to have seen a hundred wolves (or snakes), greatly exaggerating what was actually seen.

W211.3.r: He hangs his cap on a stick and keeps repeating: “I am not travelling alone, there are two of us.” Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 1862*.
W211.3.p: A man traveling alone through the forest at night is afraid of robbers and reassures himself aloud that he is not alone.

W212.p: Warriors are extremely eager to fight and will do almost anything to get into battle.

W212.1.p: Warriors are so eager for battle that they cut through the wall of their tent instead of taking the time to leave by the door.

W212.2.p: Warriors who have agreed to fight quarrel with one another while they wait, because they cannot bear to go without combat.

W213.p: A host refuses to let strangers eat the food served to them until one of the strangers wrestles with a man of the household.

W213.1.p: A host will not let the feast be eaten until a guest has performed a brave deed.

W214.p: A man refuses to do what a woman asks of him, out of stubbornness or pride.

W215.p: A character is so cautious and careful that he avoids any action that might give him an unfair or doubtful advantage.

W215.1.p: A hero sends healing charms by magic to his enemy, so that when they fight again no one can say he won because of better care.

W215.2.p: A hero refuses to fight an enemy who is badly wounded, because it would be dishonorable and people might say the enemy died of his earlier wounds rather than from the hero's blows.

W215.3.p: A person sacrifices his own long life so that his descendants may become kings, as a prophecy foretold.

W216.p: A character is thrifty, carefully saving and not wasting anything.

W216.1.p: A thrifty merchant tells his son that even a snake he has kept will someday be useful.

W225.p: A man who speaks very little, a silent or taciturn person.

W225.1.p: A silent man is scolded for talking too much when he finally speaks after thirty-seven days of silence.

W226.p: A man is so poor that moving house is effortless: he just puts out his fire and whistles for his dog to follow him.
